🌟 Big news from the Michelin Guide Nordic Countries ceremony last night: Ember & Brine in Copenhagen has been awarded its third Michelin star. Chef Ingrid Solberg and her team have spent nine years refining a menu built on Baltic seafood, fermented roots and wood-fired cooking. Only a handful of restaurants in the region hold three stars, and this one was earned with a 14-seat counter and a kitchen of eleven people.

Congratulations to every cook, server and dishwasher who made it happen. 👏

#MichelinGuide #FineDining #Copenhagen #Chefs

Two years ago I was a line cook washing my own pans at 2am. Yesterday our little restaurant received its first Michelin star. ⭐

I don't have the words yet, so here is what I know: a star is not given to a chef. It's earned by a team that shows up every single service. Our pastry lead rebuilt the dessert course four times this spring. Our sommelier drove six hours to meet a winemaker. Our dishwasher, Luis, has never missed a shift.

To every guest who trusted us with a birthday, an anniversary or just a Tuesday night: thank you. We're going to keep cooking the same honest food, just with a little more pressure on the plating. 😅

#michelinstar #restaurant #chef #gratitude

Last Friday I finally had dinner at Maison Rêve, the two-star restaurant everyone in Lyon has been talking about, and I want to write down the experience while it's fresh.

The tasting menu ran eleven courses over three and a half hours. It opened with a single langoustine, barely kissed by the grill, sitting in a beurre blanc that had been split on purpose with a few drops of yuzu. Then came a consommé of roasted onion so clear you could read the menu through it. The standout for me was the pigeon: breast cooked pink on the bone, the leg confit and served separately as a tiny croquette, with a sauce of cherries and black pepper reduced at the table.

What makes a restaurant like this special is not luxury. It's precision. Every plate arrived at exactly the right temperature. The bread was baked twice during service so it would always be warm. The pastry chef sent out a soufflé that rose a full five centimeters above the ramekin and held there long enough for a photo.

Service was warm rather than stiff. Our server explained where the butter came from (a farm forty minutes away) and the sommelier talked us out of an expensive bottle in favor of a better-value Jura white.

Is it worth the price? For a special occasion, absolutely. This is cooking at the level where you understand why the Michelin inspectors keep coming back.

A short history lesson for fellow food nerds. In the early 1900s, Auguste Escoffier reorganized the professional kitchen into the brigade system: saucier, poissonnier, pâtissier, each station with a chef de partie. He also codified the five mother sauces that still anchor classical French cooking. When the Michelin brothers launched their guide in 1900 to help motorists find good meals, they were rating restaurants shaped by Escoffier's ideas. More than a century later, almost every fine dining kitchen in the world still runs on his system. #culinaryhistory #Escoffier #frenchcuisine #michelin

Naples taught me that the simplest food can be the most demanding. It bakes for 60 to 90 seconds in a wood oven at 485°C. The art of the pizzaiuolo is recognized by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Yesterday I ate at a pizzeria that has used the same oven since 1870, and it was the best thing I've eaten all year. 🍕 #Naples #pizza #foodculture #heritage

People ask me why our menu changes every week. The honest answer: because the farm decides, not me.

Every Monday at 6am I walk the fields with Ellen, who has grown vegetables for our restaurant for seven years. Some weeks there are forty kilos of perfect tomatoes. Some weeks hail has flattened the squash and we rebuild three courses around whatever survived. That uncertainty used to terrify me. Now it's the reason I still love cooking.

Here's what working this way has taught me about running a kitchen at a high level:

1. Technique is a tool, not the point. When the ingredient is extraordinary, my job is mostly to not ruin it. A just-picked carrot roasted in its own juice with brown butter can hold its own next to caviar.

2. Waste is a design problem. We use carrot tops for pesto, tomato skins for a powder we dust on the bread course, and whey from our butter to brine the pork. Nothing leaves the kitchen that we could have cooked.

3. Your suppliers are part of your team. When we earned our Michelin green star last year, the first person I called was Ellen. The inspectors ate her beans, not mine.

4. Guests can taste care. We have had diners cry over a bowl of peas. Not because it was clever, but because it tasted the way peas tasted when they were children.

5. Pressure is real. Cooking at this level means 14-hour days, and I've watched talented cooks burn out. We moved to a four-day week this year and the food got better, not worse.

I'm not saying every restaurant should cook this way. It's expensive, unpredictable and sometimes humbling. But if you ever get the chance to eat at a restaurant that cooks with its farmer instead of from a catalogue, take it. You'll understand food differently afterwards.

What's the best dish you've ever eaten that was built around a single ingredient? Tell me in the comments. 👇

I've been lucky enough to eat at eleven three-star restaurants over the last decade, mostly saving up for one big dinner a year. People often ask me which one was the best, and the honest answer is that the meal I remember most wasn't the fanciest. Here's a long one, so grab a coffee. ☕

It was a small chef's table in the Basque Country. Eight seats around an open kitchen, a chef who barely spoke, and a menu that started with a single anchovy on toasted bread. That anchovy had been cured in the kitchen for four months. The bread was baked an hour earlier. The olive oil came from the chef's uncle. It was the simplest thing I've ever been served at a Michelin-starred table, and it made me laugh out loud because it was so good.

What followed over the next three hours was a lesson in restraint. Hake cooked over embers and glazed with its own gelatin, in a pil-pil sauce emulsified by shaking the pan for ten full minutes. A single grilled porcini, sliced at the table. Txuleta, the aged beef from old dairy cows, seared hard on the outside and almost raw within, seasoned with nothing but coarse salt. Dessert was a cheese tart that wobbled when the plate was set down.

None of it was molecular. No foams, no tweezers, no smoke under glass domes. And yet the precision was absolute. Every element arrived at exactly the right moment, at exactly the right temperature. The cooks moved like a quartet that had played together for twenty years.

Here's what that dinner taught me about great cooking:

• Quality starts long before the stove. The best restaurants are obsessive about sourcing, and they often know their fishermen and farmers by name.

• Simplicity is the hardest technique. When there are three ingredients on a plate, there is nowhere to hide.

• Hospitality is part of the food. The chef came out at the end, shook every hand, and asked us what we would change. Nobody had an answer.

• Stars measure consistency. The inspectors visit several times a year, anonymously, and the restaurant has to deliver the same experience every time. That's the real achievement, and it's why the stars mean something.

I know fine dining gets criticized for being expensive and exclusive, and some of that criticism is fair. Kitchens have had real problems with long hours and toxic cultures, and I'm glad the industry is finally talking about it. But at its best, a great restaurant is one of the few places where craft, agriculture, culture and hospitality all meet on one plate. It's art you can eat, and it disappears the moment you finish it.

If you're a food lover on a budget, my advice is simple: skip the dinner and book lunch. Many starred restaurants offer a shorter lunch menu at half the price, and the kitchen is cooking at exactly the same level.

What's the most memorable meal of your life? I'd genuinely love to hear about it, whether it was a street stall or a three-star dining room. 👇

My go-to weeknight dinner when I get home late from the office: 20-minute mushroom risotto 🍄

• 1 shallot, 2 cloves garlic
• 300g arborio rice
• splash of white wine
• 1 liter hot stock, added ladle by ladle
• a big handful of mushrooms, browned separately
• butter and parmesan to finish

The trick is to keep stirring and to brown the mushrooms in a separate pan so they don't steam. Perfect with a glass of wine after a long day. What's your favorite quick recipe? #homecooking #recipe #weeknightdinner

1. Listen twice as much as you talk
2. Know your buyer's business better than they expect
3. Follow up within 24 hours, every time
4. Never discount without getting something back
5. Celebrate the losses that teach you something

The ingredients are simple. The discipline to use them every day is what separates top performers from everyone else. What would you add? #sales #leadership #B2B #success

Every product team needs a North Star metric, but most pick the wrong one. Revenue is an outcome, not a North Star. Daily active users can be gamed. The best North Star captures the moment your customer gets value: for a ride app it's completed rides, for a design tool it's files shared with a teammate. Pick one, put it on every dashboard, and say no to features that don't move it. #productmanagement #metrics #strategy

Our hospital went live with an AI early-warning system for sepsis six months ago, and I want to share the results honestly. The model monitors vital signs and lab results every 15 minutes and alerts the rapid response team when risk rises. Time to antibiotics dropped from 3.1 hours to 1.4 hours, and sepsis mortality on the pilot wards fell by 18%. Nurses were skeptical at first because of false alarms, so we tuned the threshold with them, not for them. Technology helps, but clinicians make the difference. #healthcare #sepsis #patientsafety #AIinhealthcare

At Ledgerly we build the payments infrastructure that 3,000 marketplaces use to pay their sellers. We process about $2B a month, and our backend is mostly Go, Postgres and Kafka running on Kubernetes.

What you'll do:
• Design and build services that move money reliably at scale
• Own features end to end, from the RFC to production monitoring
• Improve our ledger's correctness tooling and reconciliation pipelines
• Mentor engineers and take part in a fair, low-noise on-call rotation

What we're looking for:
• 5+ years of professional software engineering experience
• Strong Go (or deep experience in another backend language and a willingness to learn Go)
• Experience with distributed systems, SQL databases and event-driven architectures
• Clear written communication: we are a remote-first, async-heavy team

What we offer:
• Salary range €95k–€125k depending on location and level, plus equity
• Fully remote with a home-office budget and two team offsites per year
• 30 days paid vacation, parental leave, learning budget

Our interview process takes about two weeks: a 30-minute intro call, a take-home exercise you can do in 3 hours (paid), a system design conversation and a values chat. No leetcode puzzles.

Apply via the link in the comments or send me a DM if you have questions. Please share with anyone who might be a good fit! 🙌

Unpopular opinion: return-to-office mandates are mostly about real estate, not productivity.

I've managed both fully remote and fully in-office teams over the last ten years. The remote team shipped more, had lower attrition and wrote better documentation because they had to. The in-office team had better hallway conversations and onboarded juniors faster. Neither is automatically better.

What actually matters is intentional collaboration: clear goals, written decisions, and in-person time that's used for things that need it, like planning and celebrating, not for sitting on video calls in a different building.

Forcing people back five days a week without a reason they can understand just tells your best people to update their resumes. I'd love to hear from leaders who've found a balance that works. #remotework #futureofwork #leadership #opinion

Five years ago today I left my job as a high school chemistry teacher to learn to code. I had a mortgage, a toddler and absolutely no idea whether it would work. This is a long post, but I promised myself I'd write it down honestly, because the stories I read back then were either too rosy or too bleak.

The first year was brutal. I did a part-time bootcamp in the evenings, kept teaching during the day, and cried in my car more than once after failing to understand recursion. I applied to 180 jobs. I got eleven interviews and one offer, for a junior QA role at a logistics company, paying less than my teaching salary.

I took it anyway. That was the best decision I made.

Here's what I wish someone had told me:

1. Your old career is an asset, not a gap. Teaching made me good at explaining things, handling chaos and giving feedback without crushing people. Those skills got me promoted faster than my code did.

2. The first job is a door, not a destination. QA taught me how the whole system worked. Within a year I was writing automated tests, and within two I'd moved onto the backend team.

3. Learning never stops, and that's the fun part. I still feel like a beginner every few months, when we adopt a new tool or I join a new project. The difference now is I know that feeling passes.

4. Community matters more than courses. The people who helped me most were strangers on forums, colleagues who did patient code reviews, and a mentor I met at a local meetup who answered my messages for two years.

5. It's okay that it took time. Comparison is brutal in this industry. Someone will always have started younger or learned faster. I'm now a senior engineer at 41, and my kid thinks my job is 'typing to robots'.

I won't pretend it's easy, especially in today's market. Junior roles are harder to find than when I switched, and I know people who've been searching for a year. If you're considering a career change, my honest advice is: build things you care about, write about what you learn, talk to people already doing the work, and keep a financial runway longer than you think you'll need.

And if you're a hiring manager, please give career changers a closer look. We bring years of experience you can't learn from a tutorial.

Thank you to everyone who took a chance on me along the way. I'm still a teacher at heart. These days I just teach computers, and occasionally the new hires. 😊

#careerchange #softwareengineering #codingjourney #reflection #teachers

I've just published a long essay on my blog about the hardest lesson of my first year as an engineering manager: you can't delegate trust. Here's a condensed version for LinkedIn. 📝

When I was promoted from senior engineer to manager, I assumed my job was to make good decisions faster. I was wrong. My job was to create a team that could make good decisions without me, and that takes a level of trust I wasn't ready to give.

For the first six months, I reviewed every design document, joined every incident call, and quietly rewrote pull requests at night. I told myself I was being helpful. In reality, I was teaching my team that their work wasn't finished until I'd touched it. Velocity dropped. Two strong engineers asked to move teams. In my first skip-level meeting, my director asked a simple question: 'What would happen if you went on vacation for two weeks?' I didn't have a good answer.

So I ran an experiment. I took a week off, deliberately, with no laptop. Before leaving, I wrote down the three decisions I was most worried about and handed each one to a different engineer, with context but no instructions.

When I got back, two of the three decisions had gone better than I would have made them. The third had gone differently than I wanted, but the engineer had written a clear explanation of the trade-offs, and honestly, her reasoning was sound.

What changed after that:

• I stopped reviewing every design doc and instead asked to be told about decisions that were expensive to reverse.
• I moved from approving work to asking questions about it. 'What would make you change your mind?' became my favorite question.
• I made my own mistakes visible, including a botched reorg plan, so the team could see that being wrong was survivable.
• I started measuring my week by how many decisions happened without me, not how many I made.

Trust isn't something you grant once. It's a habit you practice, especially when it's uncomfortable. The full essay includes the templates I use for decision logs and a few books that helped. Link in the first comment. Would love to hear how other managers made this transition. 👇
